search.title: About OpenTurbine
search.text: Learn what OpenTurbine provides for supported ESP32 turbine-controller projects, including open-source firmware, browser setup, documentation, and Windows installation.

search.title: What the project includes
search.text: The project includes firmware, a browser interface, configuration/calibration tools and the Windows installer. Check supported hardware and electrical requirements before choosing parts. OpenTurbine is developed in the open. Releases, issue templates, and source history are available on GitHub. Read the safety notice before powering or connecting any real hardware.

search.title: Explore a basic single-shaft turbine system
search.text: Walk through an ordinary OpenTurbine single-shaft example to understand the hardware, controllers, calibration, sequence, and safety decisions without copying engine-specific limits.

search.title: What this example contains
search.context: Explore a basic single-shaft turbine system
search.text: Part of the system Example choice Why it is present ECU Supported Classic ESP32 or ESP32-S3 board Runs OpenTurbine and hosts the local browser interface. Shaft feedback One conditioned N1 speed signal Shows core speed and supports acceleration checks, idle control, pullback, and independent overspeed shutdown. Gas temperature K-type thermocouple through a supported converter Shows turbine temperature and supports hot-start and overtemperature protection. Lubrication feedback Conditioned oil-pressure sensor Confirms pressure during startup and allows running oil-pressure protection or regulation. Operator demand Potentiometer or RC PWM throttle input Provides the requested running demand after calibration. A logging-only or externally controlled system can omit it. Main fuel metering Rated pump driver, ESC, or metering-valve interface Receives the protected proportional fuel command. The ESP32 pin is only a control signal. Fuel isolation Normally closed shutoff valve through a rated driver Provides a separate physical fuel-isolation command during stop and fault handling. Starting Electric starter and, where required, a separate starter-enable output Cranks the engine while the startup sequence checks time, speed, and temperature progress. Ignition Igniter through its specified isolated driver Provides ignition energy only during the configured startup stages. Oil delivery Relay or proportional oil-pump driver Primes before rotation, supports the run, and can continue through cooldown. Independent stop Hard-wired emergency-stop circuit Removes fuel or relevant load power without relying on the ESP32, Wi-Fi, browser, or software. The hardware compatibility table lists the converter and expansion chips currently supported. A compatible interface still needs suitable voltage levels, signal conditioning, load drivers, fusing, grounding, and transient protection.

search.title: How the signals fit together
search.context: Explore a basic single-shaft turbine system
search.text: 1. N1, turbine temperature, and oil pressure enter the ECU through suitable conditioners or supported converter modules. 2. Throttle demand asks for fuel; it does not bypass controller limits or shutdown logic. 3. Main Fuel Metering receives the final protected proportional demand. 4. Fuel Shutoff, Starter, Igniter, and Oil Pump are operated by the startup/shutdown sequence and applicable built-in subsystems. 5. The independent emergency stop removes energy outside the software path. The browser is used to configure and observe the ECU. Losing the browser or Wi-Fi does not become a new engine command, but an operating installation must never depend on the browser as its only stop method.

search.title: Build the example in the interface
search.context: Explore a basic single-shaft turbine system
search.text: You can explore this layout on a spare supported board with every load supply disconnected.

search.title: 1. Hardware
search.context: Explore a basic single-shaft turbine system
search.text: Add only the devices in the example inventory. For every channel, choose the real electrical signal type and a valid pin for the selected board. A relay is binary; PWM and servo/ESC signals are proportional. Resolve every pin conflict and missing electrical requirement before saving. Do not copy pin numbers from another board or installation. Classic ESP32 and ESP32-S3 have different usable pins, and a PCB profile may own its connections.

search.title: 2. Controllers
search.context: Explore a basic single-shaft turbine system
search.text: Open the existing Main Fuel Metering controller. If none owns that output yet, create it under Controllers → Output controllers → + Create controller; use the illustrated steps. A straightforward starting point is operator demand commanding the fuel output, with engine-specific limits and automatic idle left for later commissioning. Choose Running Idle Mode deliberately. Off adds no Running floor; Fixed, Input channel and Automatic Idle each provide one differently. Older files needing an explicit mode choice retain their behavior until you change Idle settings. See the idle choices before setting the mapped minimum. If the oil pump is proportional and oil pressure is fitted, it may use an oil-pressure controller. A relay oil pump remains simple On/Off sequence hardware. Leave optional behavior disabled until its feedback and purpose are understood.

search.title: 3. Calibration
search.context: Explore a basic single-shaft turbine system
search.text: Calibrate the throttle endpoints, verify N1 against an independent tachometer, compare turbine temperature with a trusted reference, and calibrate oil pressure at zero and against a gauge. Calibration makes a reading meaningful; it does not prove that a chosen safety limit is suitable.

search.title: 4. Sequence
search.context: Explore a basic single-shaft turbine system
search.text: A typical startup concept is: Standby → pre-oil → crank → ignition → introduce fuel → confirm light-off → accelerate → final checks → running A typical shutdown concept is: Remove fuel and ignition → allow speed/temperature to fall → continue required oil or cooldown actions → stop all outputs The exact order can vary with the engine and starting system. Every wait needs a finite timeout and safe failure result. Do not copy example delays or demands from an unrelated turbine.

search.title: 5. Protection
search.context: Explore a basic single-shaft turbine system
search.text: Enable a protection only after its input is fitted, calibrated, and proven healthy. Keep these ideas separate: - Pullback gradually reduces fuel as a measured value approaches a configured boundary. - Hard shutdown removes combustion authority when its independently configured trip condition is confirmed. - Reduced-Power operation is a deliberate degraded option for eligible feedback failures; it is not a replacement for a working stop path.

search.title: 6. Dry test
search.context: Explore a basic single-shaft turbine system
search.text: With fuel, ignition energy, starter power, and other load power isolated, verify: - every input moves in the expected direction and reports believable units; - each output uses the expected pin, polarity, signal type, and parked state; - START advances only through conditions that are intentionally satisfied; - sensor loss produces the expected warning, Reduced-Power choice, or lock; - STOP, overspeed, overtemperature, and other configured trips remove the intended commands; and - the independent emergency stop removes energy even if the ECU is unavailable.

search.title: What to change for other systems
search.context: Explore a basic single-shaft turbine system
search.text: - A logging-only installation can omit fuel metering and every actuator; fit only the measurements that should be recorded. - An air-start system replaces the electric starter path with its valve and interlocks. - A free-turbine or turboprop system adds N2 and may assign a governor to fuel or propeller pitch. - An afterburning system adds separate fuel and ignition hardware plus explicit arm, light-off evidence, and shutdown sequencing. - A sensor-light manual system can retain external fuel control while using OpenTurbine for sequencing, selected protection, or logging. These remain the same product: Hardware describes what exists, Controllers describe normal ownership, Sequence describes state changes, and System contains ECU-wide behavior.

search.title: OpenTurbine FAQ: boards, installation and updates
search.text: Answers about supported ESP32 boards, Windows installation, hardware channels, controllers, updates, backups, wiring, logs, and experimental-use limits for OpenTurbine.

search.title: Do I need programming experience? Do I download the source ZIP?
search.context: OpenTurbine FAQ: boards, installation and updates
search.text: No. Download OpenTurbineSetupTool.exe from the official release. Do not use GitHub’s Download ZIP source-code button for normal Windows setup.

search.title: Which boards are supported?
search.context: OpenTurbine FAQ: boards, installation and updates
search.text: Use a Classic ESP32 with at least 4 MB flash, or an ESP32-S3 DevKitC-1-compatible board with at least 8 MB flash. The same universal S3 image runs on 8 MB and 16 MB modules and does not require PSRAM. ESP32-C3 and other unlisted ESP32 families are not supported by the current normal setup path.

search.title: Does driver installation require a restart?
search.context: OpenTurbine FAQ: boards, installation and updates
search.text: Usually not. The Setup Tool rescans after installing a driver and shows when Windows specifically requires a restart. If the connected CP210x/WCH bridge has no COM port, it offers the matching driver even when an unrelated COM port exists.

search.title: What does Clean install erase? How does Update keep my setup?
search.context: OpenTurbine FAQ: boards, installation and updates
search.text: Clean install/reinstall erases the selected board. Update and keep my setup is the normal Wi-Fi update path for a working controller; it backs up the engine file first. Keep backups private because they can contain Wi-Fi credentials.

search.title: Can I reuse a pre-2.0 engine file?
search.context: OpenTurbine FAQ: boards, installation and updates
search.text: OpenTurbine 2.0 intentionally replaces older hardware and startup-safety behavior. Keep the old file as a reference, but use a clean installation and rebuild/review Hardware, Controllers, System, Calibration, Sequence, and every dry shutdown test. Read the v2 migration guide before moving an engine installation.

search.title: Can I explore without a turbine? Can GPIO power a pump or igniter?
search.context: OpenTurbine FAQ: boards, installation and updates
search.text: You can explore and configure the dashboard with loads physically disconnected. GPIO pins are 3.3 V logic only: they do not power pumps, valves, starters, or ignition. Use suitable protected driver electronics.

search.title: Can I add a sensor or output that is not one of the built-in names?
search.context: OpenTurbine FAQ: boards, installation and updates
search.text: Yes. In Hardware, add a generic input or output with a readable name, the correct signal type, connection, range and safe states. Use that displayed device name when selecting it in Controllers, Sequence or Tools. Its electrical interface still needs suitable conditioning or a rated driver.

search.title: What can simple controls do?
search.context: OpenTurbine FAQ: boards, installation and updates
search.text: Simple controls live with the other output owners on Controllers. A control can switch an output at a sensor threshold with hysteresis or map an input range directly to a variable PWM/servo output range. Each output has one normal owner; Sequence owns ordered startup/shutdown actions and safety can always override normal demand.

search.title: Why does Windows warn about the Setup Tool?
search.context: OpenTurbine FAQ: boards, installation and updates
search.text: Use the official OpenTurbine download link and choose More info → Run anyway when Windows offers it. Do not disable Windows security or use an installer from another website. Normal installation does not require understanding checksums; the Setup Tool automatically verifies the firmware package it downloads.

search.title: Where are logs and complete instructions?
search.context: OpenTurbine FAQ: boards, installation and updates
search.text: Setup Tool diagnostics are under %LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenTurbine\SetupTool\logs. The User Guide and reference covers operating and wiring details. Use Setup Help for installation problems.

search.title: Is OpenTurbine certified or inherently safe? Does it work on macOS/Linux?
search.context: OpenTurbine FAQ: boards, installation and updates
search.text: No. It is experimental and requires independently verified limits, drivers, and physical shutdown protection. There is no graphical macOS/Linux installer; manual PlatformIO builds are an advanced/developer path.

search.title: Install OpenTurbine from Windows
search.text: Install OpenTurbine on a supported ESP32 using the Windows Setup Tool, then connect to its Wi-Fi dashboard.

search.title: 1. Prepare the board
search.text: You need: - A Classic ESP32 board with at least 4 MB flash, or an ESP32-S3 DevKitC-1-compatible board with at least 8 MB flash. The universal S3 image runs on 8 MB and 16 MB modules and does not require PSRAM. - A Windows computer. - A USB data cable. A charge-only cable can power the board but cannot install firmware. Keep fuel, ignition energy, starter power and actuator/load power physically disconnected during installation.

search.title: 2. Download the Setup Tool
search.text: Download OpenTurbineSetupTool.exe for Windows. Use the executable above, not GitHub's Download ZIP source-code button. If Windows displays a warning, confirm that the file came from the official OpenTurbine Releases page before using More info → Run anyway. Do not disable Windows protection globally. Expected: Windows opens the OpenTurbine Setup Tool.

search.title: 3. Connect and identify the board
search.text: Connect the ESP32 directly to the computer and open the Setup Tool. It will show a detected board or identify a missing CP210x/WCH USB driver. If a driver is required, use the matching option offered by the Setup Tool. If Windows already shows a COM port but the board does not answer, close other serial programs, hold BOOT, tap EN/RESET, and try again. Expected: the Setup Tool shows the connected board and a usable COM port. No board or COM port? Use the board-detection troubleshooting steps.

search.title: 4. Choose install or update
search.text: - For a new board, select Clean install / reinstall. This erases the selected board. - For a working OpenTurbine ECU, select Update and keep my setup. Back up the engine file first; this path is designed to preserve the setup. Check the selected board and operation before starting. Do not disconnect USB power while the Setup Tool is writing firmware. Expected: installation completes without an error and the board restarts. Installation stopped or failed? Go directly to flashing help.

search.title: 5. Open the dashboard
search.text: Join the Wi-Fi network created by the board, remain connected even if Windows says the network has no internet, and open http://192.168.4.1 in a browser. Expected: the OpenTurbine dashboard loads and shows the ECU state. Wi-Fi missing or dashboard not loading? See Wi-Fi help or dashboard help .

search.title: 6. Continue with your own hardware
search.text: OpenTurbine does not require one fixed engine layout. Describe only the sensors and actuators your system actually has, then configure and test them in this order: Hardware → Controllers → System → Calibration → Sequence → Tools → Dashboard Start with Level 1: build a basic system for wiring, configured cards and checks in order. The complete User Guide is the detailed reference; the single-shaft overview shows the overall relationships. Do not connect fuel or ignition energy until the independent stop and every configured shutdown path have been dry-tested. Begin Level 1 Open the User Guide Hardware requirements Troubleshooting

search.title: Build 1 Configure a basic turbojet
search.text: Configure one HX80-sized teaching turbojet with starter, fuel, ignition, lubrication, essential protection and a complete dry startup and shutdown walkthrough.

search.title: What you will build
search.text: Our example is a homemade, HX80-sized turbojet: one compressor/turbine shaft, liquid fuel, spark ignition and an electric starter. OpenTurbine commands its fuel pump, starter, ignition, oil pump and fuel shutoff. A separate free power turbine comes in Build 3. Normal full-power readings are about RPM N1, 3–4 bar combustor pressure and 4–5 bar oil pressure. N1 means gas-generator shaft speed. TOT means temperature measured after its turbine. Pressure examples use bar gauge, measured above atmospheric pressure. Fuel delivery pressure is a different measurement. Example numbers teach configuration. The engine worksheet distinguishes these operating readings from assumed idle, fuel and protection values. Replace assumed settings with your engine's verified data before live operation. The guide configures an existing engine; it does not design its combustor, bearings or starter coupling. Start with installation, the parts and pin tables and a meter. During initial checks, disconnect real fuel, ignition energy and starter power; use signal observation or suitable dummy loads. An independent physical stop must remove hazardous energy without the ECU or browser. Lubrication is part of the installation from the beginning.

search.title: 1 · Connect the ECU and Start/Stop
search.text: An input reports a measurement or request. An output sends a command to a driver, which switches load power. GPIO means a numbered signal pin on the ESP32; it does not supply a pump or starter. 1. Power the board by USB alone for this first check. Open OpenTurbine and select the correct target/profile in Hardware. 2. Back up an existing setup using System → Maintenance → Full engine file backup / restore. Review preloaded channels; edit matching ones and remove unfitted examples before adding devices. Assign each physical device once. 3. Choose your board's column in the connection table. Follow signal names; S3 GPIO numbers are not Classic GPIO numbers. 4. Edit Start and Stop in Hardware. Connect each momentary dry contact from its assigned GPIO to GND. Select Active LOW, enable Pull-up and leave Pull-down off. Save and allow the restart. Check: both contacts read inactive when released and active when pressed. Release Start after boot before trying a new press. These are ECU commands, separate from the physical energy-removing stop. Classic GPIO34–39 have no internal pull-ups; the example assigns the buttons elsewhere.

search.title: 2 · Add speed, temperature and throttle
search.text: Add one input at a time in Hardware → Add input. Save, then check its reading before continuing. N1 speed. Select N1 speed, name it N1 Speed, choose Pulse / frequency input and assign its GPIO. Enter the pickup's actual pulses per revolution (PPR). The example uses one counted pulse per revolution. Its conditioner supplies clean 3.3 V-compatible pulses; raw magnetic pickups and 5 V outputs need conditioning. The diagram uses an external pull-up. For compatible short bench wiring, Input bias → Pull-up can supply bias on a suitable pin instead. Verify pulse quality at the required rate. At RPM and 1 PPR, a generator supplies 1000 Hz; at 100 Hz the display should show 6000 RPM. Compare against an independent reference. A stationary magnet does not generate continuing RPM. Exhaust temperature. Connect a K-type probe to a matching MAX31855 converter, not directly to GPIO. In Hardware → Shared sensor buses → Edit buses, enable SPI, assign SCK and MISO and save. This converter does not use MOSI. Add TOT / EGT, name it Main TOT, choose MAX31855 and assign its separate CS pin. Check: a healthy room-temperature reading, rising with gentle warming and falling with cooling. Check probe polarity if incorrect. This proves basic response, not high-temperature accuracy. Throttle. Wire a 10 kΩ linear potentiometer with its ends at 3.3 V and GND and its wiper at the throttle ADC pin. Add Throttle Input → Analog voltage input (ADC) and save. On Calibration, jump to Throttle Input, hold the knob at intended minimum and select Capture Min; repeat with Capture Max, then Save. Check: minimum/middle/maximum give about 0%/50%/100% smoothly. If reversed, correct Hardware → Throttle Input → Input direction and verify again. Classic ADC inputs here use ADC1 for Wi-Fi compatibility.

search.title: 3 · Add oil-pressure feedback
search.text: The example uses a 0–10 bar gauge transducer with 0.5–4.5 V output. Its specified supply powers it; a divider conditions its output. Do not connect 4.5 V directly to GPIO. 1. Add Oil Pressure → Analog voltage input (ADC), assign its ADC GPIO and save. 2. Open Calibration → Oil Pressure. Leave Include electric oil-pump control and minimum-output calibration unchecked for Sensor only mode. It uses your external pressure source and sends no pump commands. Select 0 bar (gauge pressure) for this sensor. 3. With the circuit safely depressurized, press Start Calibration to capture ambient. Apply a known pressure measured by a trusted gauge, enter it and select Capture point. Repeat at another point, select a straight-line fit for this sensor, then select Compute Fit → and Save calibration. Release pressure and verify zero. For this circuit, zero is mV and sensitivity mV/bar at the ADC. bar corresponds to 920 mV. Verify your actual transducer and gauge instead of assuming identical calibration. Optional pump-assisted calibration is separate and can operate the pump. Check: zero and at least two reference pressures agree with the gauge, returning to zero afterward. An incorrectly scaled reading is not ready for protection.

search.title: 4 · Add and test the five outputs
search.text: Use rated external drivers and separate fused load power. Keep load current out of sensor grounds. Join references where required by nonisolated interfaces; follow module documentation for isolated ones. | Add output / name | Example interface | Establish before saving | | --- | --- | --- | | Starter | RC servo / ESC pulse | Actual endpoints/arming; logical zero stops it | | Main Fuel Metering | High-frequency duty PWM | Compatible frequency, polarity, physical off at 0% | | Igniter | On/off driver | Spark command polarity and de-energized state | | Oil Pump | High-frequency duty PWM | Ratings, direction and permitted command range | | Fuel Shutoff | On/off driver | Open/closed direction and de-energized isolation | For each, choose Hardware → Add output, its named purpose, driver and GPIO, then save. The teaching PWM driver accepts Hz, bits; match your driver. ESC pulses are a different signal from duty PWM. For each output, open Tools → Tool settings, review short test duration and demand, save, then run its test. Begin with dummy loads or signal measurement. Check physical direction and return to the safe state after expiry. Prove shutoff direction with a benign unpressurized test. A relay click does not prove valve state. Calibrate the actual fuel pump through Calibration → Minimum Reliable Fuel-Metering Output on an isolated flow rig. Follow sweep, stop and repeatable-restart prompts. Do not run it dry unless permitted. This measures reliable metering, not engine idle. The assumed teaching results are % reliable minimum and % idle; your measurements replace both.

search.title: 5 · Give fuel and oil their normal commands
search.text: Hardware describes connections; Controllers defines normal control; Sequence handles transitions. Configure one normal controller per output. In Controllers → Output controllers → + Create controller, choose Main Fuel Metering, create it if absent, and open it: | Setting | Teaching configuration | | --- | --- | | Controller name | Main Fuel | | Control method / Controlled by | Map input to output / Throttle Input | | Input low / high | 0% / 100% | | Output low / high | % / % | | Activate when | Entering Running | | Deactivate when | Entering Shutdown and Entering Standby | Under Fuel-metering support → Idle, select Off — no idle floor. Mapping Output low supplies this example's simple idle command; no extra idle method is needed. Save. Throttle requests fuel, not a guaranteed RPM. For oil, edit the existing pressure controller if one is already assigned to Oil Pump. Otherwise use the creator's separate Oil pump and Pressure feedback selectors, then Create oil-pressure controller. Open Oil Pump → Oil Pressure Control. Select Oil Pressure, the matching pump, Pressure target set by → Fixed pressure, and bar. Set its Low-pressure threshold to bar and Low-pressure confirmation to ms. Verify command bounds and failure responses against the oil rig. Use Normal fault shutdown for the teaching feedback-loss/low-pressure responses; Build 2 explains the full card. Check: on an appropriate oil circuit, establish target pressure without excessive overshoot and compare the gauge. Response gain and pump duty depend on the pump. The sequence establishes lubrication before ignition and retains it during shutdown.

search.title: 6 · Set essential protection
search.text: Open Controllers → Shutdown & Protection. These are assumed teaching thresholds; replace them with verified engine settings before operation: | Card | Value and enable state | | --- | --- | | N1 core speed | Maximum N1 Speed RPM; overspeed ON | | Temperature protection | Temperature Source for Safeties = Turbine outlet temperature (TOT), using Main TOT; outlet limit °C; running shutdown ON | | Oil pressure protection | Low-Pressure Limit bar; confirmation ms; monitor Running; ON | Startup's oil check comes next. It permits pressure to build before ignition without treating zero Standby pressure as a running fault. With separate startup-temperature guard OFF, normal temperature shutdown applies during Startup too. Build 2 teaches a separate guard. Dashboard: retained N1/temperature limits set approach colours. Shutdown has its own enable switch; a marker is not proof of a physical trip test. Find limits through Dashboard → Edit cards → Edit limit & safety, or Controllers. Build 2 covers pressure markers and limiting.

search.title: 7 · Build startup and shutdown
search.text: Open Sequence → Startup, reviewing any defaults before replacement. Choose + Add block, add the stated type, open its card and set the fields. Use the grip to reorder. Device commands are ACTION entries; Set Starter — UNTIL waits for N1. | Order | Startup block | Teaching setting / purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | Build Oil Pressure | Target bar; minimum ; timeout ms | | 2 | Set Starter — UNTIL | %, ramp %/s; N1 ; timeout ms | | 3 | Set Igniter — ACTION | ON | | 4 | Set Fuel Shutoff — ACTION | Open; verify actual command polarity | | 5 | Set Main Fuel Metering — ACTION | % assumed starting fuel | | 6 | Confirm Combustion by Temperature | °C; timeout ms | | 7 | Final Startup Checks | Require N1 ≥ RPM, oil ≥ bar, TOT ≥ °C; stable ms; timeout ms | | 8 | Set Starter — ACTION | 0% | | 9 | Set Igniter — ACTION | OFF | | 10 | Final Startup Checks | Repeat after starter release to verify sustained operation | Both Final Startup Checks instances share settings. Leave their optional output-release switches off: explicit actions perform release. The second check must pass without starter assistance. This path uses an explicit fuel command instead of Accelerate to Idle, whose built-in fuel behavior is different. On Shutdown, add Immediate Fuel and Ignition Cut → Wait for Rotor to Slow → Cooldown → Wait for Complete Stop. Fuel and ignition cut first. Set the N1-drop threshold below the actual starter's safe re-engagement speed. In Cooldown, choose oil pumping ON, bar target and °C temperature target; starter cooling stays OFF unless its mechanism supports it. Give every wait a finite, engine-appropriate timeout. Shutdown can continue after cooling timeout: check final oil behavior deliberately. Save and reopen both paths. This release can show SafetyHold present but no Spool block for this explicit-command path. Check that the Starter 0% action is present before the second Final Startup Checks and that the final preview shows Starter 0%; then confirm the reviewed warning. A missing starter cut or missing sensor evidence must be corrected. Startup fuel should point to the Running controller; shutdown behavior must match the installation.

search.title: 8 · Prove the setup and save it
search.text: Keep hazardous energy isolated. Use safe signal sources or simulation for conditions you cannot produce physically; do not bypass protection to force a test through. - Verify each input, calibration, output direction and physical off state. - Follow Startup with valid evidence: oil before ignition and stable checks after starter release. - Leave a required condition unsatisfied: its timeout must produce the stated abort/fault and fuel cut. - Test STOP during startup and Running. Check physical isolation and lubrication, not just the mode label. - Exercise feedback loss and inspect the reason and output response. Reduced power does not restore missing protection. - Save/reload and download the engine file from System → Maintenance → Full engine file backup / restore. Label it Build 1 — basic turbojet, recording physical versus simulated checks. You have one coherent configuration and know where its settings belong. Actual commissioning needs the engine's measured limits and verified starting behavior. Alternative methods belong in the User Guide and optional workshops. Parts and worksheet Build 2 →

search.title: Build 2 Improve control and protection
search.text: Develop the same turbojet with combustor-pressure measurement, automatic idle, oil feedback, fuel limiting, startup protection and sequencer-controlled safety logic.

search.title: Start from the basic turbojet
search.text: You should have the Build 1 checklist completed and its engine-file backup saved. Reuse its channels. The only required new measurement here is Combustor Pressure; the second-circuit switch exercise is optional. Do not create another fuel or oil pump entry. The same teaching worksheet supplies the example numbers. RPM full-power N1, 3–4 bar combustor pressure and 4–5 bar oil pressure describe normal operation. Other numbers are assumed examples, requiring verification for an actual engine.

search.title: 1 · Add combustor pressure
search.text: This pressure is measured at the identified combustor tap, in bar gauge for the example. It is not fuel delivery pressure or oil supply pressure. Use plumbing and a transducer arrangement rated for the gas, temperature and pressure; the ECU guide covers its electrical signal, not hot-gas plumbing design. 1. Reuse the conditioned pressure-input pattern with a separate sensor and ADC pin. 2. In Hardware → Add input, choose Pressure 1 / P1, name it Combustor Pressure, select Analog voltage input (ADC) and assign its GPIO. Save. 3. With a trusted gauge, measure ADC-pin voltage at depressurized zero and a known pressure. In Hardware → Combustor Pressure → Edit, enter Zero offset (mV) and mV per bar, then save. Sensitivity = (reference ADC mV − zero ADC mV) ÷ reference bar. The illustrated circuit gives (760 − 200) ÷ 3.5 = 160 mV/bar; use your measured values and verify another pressure. Check: depressurized gauge zero and at least two known points agree with the reference. At the example's bar nominal pressure, the illustrated ADC signal is 760 mV. A sensor's 10 bar measuring range is not the engine's pressure limit.

search.title: 2 · Add automatic idle
search.text: Build 1 maps the lowest throttle position to a fixed % fuel command. Automatic idle instead adjusts the Running fuel floor to hold a measured speed. This helps explain feedback: target speed → compare actual N1 → adjust fuel → change N1. 1. Open Controllers → Main Fuel and change mapped Output low to the measured reliable pump minimum ( % in the teaching dataset). Leave Output high at % and the Running activation unchanged. 2. Open Fuel-metering support → Idle, select Running Idle Mode → Automatic Idle, and select N1 Speed as feedback. 3. Enter the example settings below. Keep the standard method initially; predictive settings are a later tuning choice. | Field | Teaching value | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | Idle Target (N1/N2) | RPM | Desired idle, not full-power speed | | No-Correction Band | RPM | Avoids correcting every small fluctuation | | Stop Controlling Above | RPM | Releases added idle correction above this speed | | Maximum Normal Idle Fuel Output | % | Base limit on idle authority | | Maximum Fuel Range Multiplier | 1 | Keeps this example's ceiling at % | Open Response tuning, review Fuel Increase/Decrease Time and save. Their correct values depend on engine response; slower changes give more time to observe a controlled test. A simulator can prove field selection and limits, not tune a real rotor. Test correction direction, settling and fuel bounds with an appropriate test setup before relying on the loop. Check: below the target, idle may add fuel within its authority. It must not demand beyond the ceiling; above the cutoff it releases its added floor. Verify feedback-loss response, STOP and handover. An unhealthy input does not supply valid closed-loop control. Other idle choices: Off uses the mapped low command; Fixed fuel percentage supplies a separate Running floor; Input channel follows a selected calibrated input. They are alternatives, not additional required controllers. Their full procedures are in the Idle reference.

search.title: 3 · Understand and verify oil feedback
search.text: Open Controllers → Oil Pump → Oil Pressure Control, the controller already created in Build 1. Keep Pressure feedback = Oil Pressure, Controlled pump = Oil Pump, Pressure target set by = Fixed pressure, Pressure target = bar. Variable targets based on fuel demand or shaft speed are optional; the basic engine does not need them to explain a pressure loop. | Group | What to establish | | --- | --- | | Pressure deadband | A small tolerated pressure error; example bar | | Minimum / maximum pump command | Repeatable pump operation and permitted driver authority, measured on the rig | | Response gain | How strongly demand changes with pressure error; tune without excessive overshoot or cycling | | Feedback-loss delay / command | How long loss must persist and what bounded pump command is used afterward | | Low-pressure threshold / confirmation | Separate from target; example bar for ms | | Failure responses | Warning, normal fault shutdown or immediate dry-oil stop, selected deliberately | Normal fault shutdown cuts combustion and follows the configured shutdown handling. Immediate dry-oil stop has a different output policy, including a bounded selected-pump run; read its displayed explanation before choosing it. A higher pump command cannot cure an empty tank, broken line or failed pump. There are two possible sources of a low-oil response: this loop's own low-pressure monitoring, and Shutdown & Protection → Oil pressure protection. Review both and align their thresholds/times deliberately. The teaching loop and general protection use the same bar/ ms example; do not leave a second unseen threshold fighting the intended policy. The general protection's selected phases do not change the loop's independent failure behavior. Check: confirm input/output direction separately, then a small target change on a suitable nonhazardous oil rig. Observe settling, bounds, low pressure, lost feedback and recovery. Repeat the startup prime and shutdown lubrication checks after tuning. Save and reload.

search.title: 4 · Separate display, limiting and shutdown
search.text: Open Controllers → Shutdown & Protection → Combustor Pressure protection. Three concepts must stay distinct: | Function | Result | Teaching pressure example | | --- | --- | --- | | Dashboard reference | Scale, approach colours and limit marker | Retained bar high-pressure limit | | Fuel limiting | Gradually reduces fuel as pressure rises | Begin bar; full reduction bar | | Fault shutdown | Cuts combustion after the confirmed trip | ON, bar, 500 ms confirmation | 1. Set the retained pressure limit. Turn Fault shutdown ON and set its confirmation time. 2. Turn Fuel limiting ON. Choose Simple — measured value first; enter Begin/Full values and review Reduction Strength. Predictive additionally uses rate of change and needs separate validation. 3. Save and compare the Dashboard. With a positive saved limit, P1/P2/torque bars use its reference, colours and limit marker. With no positive limit they use automatic range. Switching shutdown OFF preserves the saved reference and advisory display; it only disables automatic shutdown. N1 and engine temperature also use retained reference limits for colours; their shutdown marker follows enable state. Find fields via Dashboard → Edit cards → Edit limit & safety. Manual instrument scale preferences do not recalibrate a sensor or enable protection. Oil pressure is a low-limit instrument: do not copy a high-pressure trip interpretation onto it. For temperature limiting, the teaching band is – °C below the °C running trip. For each real limit, verify an approach, a confirmed trip and the disabled/advisory state using safe test inputs.

search.title: 5 · Give Startup its own temperature guard
search.text: Some engines have a justified transient starting-temperature envelope different from their running limit. Open Shutdown & Protection → Temperature protection → Startup protection and enable Separate startup temperature guard only when your engine's data supports that distinction. | Teaching setting | Value | | --- | --- | | Immediate startup overtemperature | ON, °C | | Sustained startup temperature | ON, °C | | Allowed time above threshold | ms | With this guard enabled, normal temperature shutdown and temperature fuel limiting apply in Running; the separate guard protects Startup. With it OFF, normal temperature protection/limiting also apply during Startup. Other protections are not automatically suspended by this temperature choice. A sustained-temperature trip does not measure acceleration. Keep the N1/finite-time startup checks from Build 1 to detect failure to reach the required speed. Test immediate trip, sustained trip, cooling below the dwell threshold and a failed acceleration separately. The Hot engine start interlock in the temperature card is another decision: it checks temperature before starting. The example pre-start maximum is °C. It is not the ignition-confirmation temperature or a startup overtemperature threshold. Verify it blocks a hot start and accepts a healthy cool input.

search.title: 6 · Make a named switch safety controller
search.text: Optional example: a second oil circuit has its own switch. Add it only if you want to learn a separate controller; do not duplicate the existing oil measurement as another hidden protection. 1. Wire a dry contact using the Start/Stop pattern. Choose Hardware → Add input → Generic digital input, name it Oil circuit 2 switch, select On/off switch input, assign its GPIO and set polarity so ON means pressure fault. Check both physical states. 2. In Controllers → + Create controller, choose Request Fault Shutdown and create a controller named Oil circuit 2. 3. Select Controlled by → Oil circuit 2 switch and Control method → Switch state. Choose the request condition Switch is ON and a 500 ms confirmation. A switch has no analogue switch point or hysteresis to tune. 4. Choose Activate when → Entering Running; choose Deactivate when → Entering Shutdown / Entering Standby. Save and reload. Check: a brief contact disturbance shorter than confirmation does not trip, a sustained fault does, and the displayed reason identifies this controller. Test in each chosen phase. An active pressure-fault switch while stopped should not become an unintended Standby fault; monitoring starts at the selected event. Inspect the consequences of a broken wire—simple contacts are not supervised circuits.

search.title: 7 · Place controller activation in Sequence
search.text: Entering a mode is convenient; sometimes a controller should start at an exact point inside Startup. To learn this, edit the optional Oil circuit 2 controller: select Activate when → Sequencer block instead of Entering Running. Keep Shutdown/Standby deactivation. Save and read the sequence-placement notice. 1. Open Sequence. The Controller blocks — needs placement area contains Activate Oil circuit 2. 2. Drag it into Startup after the stage that establishes pressure in the monitored circuit, before fuel admission. After Build Oil Pressure is appropriate only if that block supplies this circuit too; an independent circuit needs its own preparation. 3. If you also select Deactivate when → Sequencer block, drag its separate Deactivate card to the intended location. An unused card stays in the placement area. 4. To move a placed block to another path, remove it and drag it back from the placement area. Save only after all required blocks are placed; check the editor's explanation if a controller is incomplete. When an output controller is active, conflicting sequence commands for its output are ghosted with a reason. Deactivation sends the Hardware safe demand before releasing ownership; later discrete blocks can then command that output. Fault/STOP handling remains authoritative. A Request Fault Shutdown controller is a virtual action, not ownership of a physical fuel-pump output.

search.title: 8 · Check the changes and save Build 2
search.text: Repeat the affected dry checks: calibrated P1 readings, idle correction/limits, oil feedback and loss policy, gradual limiting versus hard trip, startup-temperature envelope, switch confirmation and controller placement. Verify the normal start/stop path again after changing control or activation. Save/reload and download Build 2 — controlled turbojet. You should be able to point to a reading, its ordinary controller, its limiting behavior and its independent shutdown setting. Continue to Build 3 for a second shaft; extra sensors are optional workshops. Fuel isolation and basic oil delivery are part of Build 1. ← Build 1 Build 3 →

search.title: Build 3 Add a free power turbine
search.text: Extend the same turbojet with a separate N2 shaft, a feedback governor, independent overspeed protection and optional instruments.

search.title: What changes in this build
search.context: Build 3 Add a free power turbine
search.text: Start with the tested Build 2 configuration and backup. The gas generator still has its N1 shaft, fuel system, ignition and oil system. A free power turbine extracts energy from its exhaust and drives a separate load. It is mechanically independent of the compressor shaft; its measured speed is N2. The mechanical turbine, containment, coupling, load and lubrication must already be designed for this installation. Adding a sensor or governor does not establish their ratings. Check whether the second stage needs an additional oil circuit; configure and test it using the same pump/pressure patterns before rotation. The gas generator's normal full-power example is RPM. That does not establish N2's speed. For this lesson only, assume a power shaft with RPM normal governed speed and RPM hard trip. These are teaching assumptions, independent of a gearbox's output speed. Use the worksheet for the actual shaft and gearbox values.

search.title: 1 · Add and identify N2
search.context: Build 3 Add a free power turbine
search.text: Reuse the conditioned N1 pulse-input pattern on a separate pin. Select a pickup and conditioner suitable for the actual shaft speed, target and environment. Do not reuse N1's electrical signal as N2. 1. In Hardware → Add input, choose N2 speed, name it N2 Power Shaft, select the pulse interface and assign its GPIO. 2. Enter the actual counted pulses per shaft revolution. If sensing after gearing, account for that ratio so the channel represents the shaft named in the guide. Write the relationship on the worksheet. 3. Match the input bias to the conditioner. Open-drain needs an appropriate pull-up; push-pull typically does not. A raw magnetic pickup requires conditioning, not just a pull-up. 4. Save, reopen and check the configured card. Check: drive N1 and N2 test inputs independently. Only the intended instrument should change. For an exact 1 PPR input, RPM equals frequency in Hz × 60; RPM needs about 333.33 Hz. Verify against an independent reference at more than one point. During a rotating/test-signal check, verify the configured loss-of-N2 response. Zero RPM while legitimately stopped is different from losing expected running feedback.

search.title: 2 · Give N2 its own protection
search.context: Build 3 Add a free power turbine
search.text: Open Controllers → Shutdown & Protection → N2 Power Shaft protection. Set Maximum N2 Speed = RPM for the teaching dataset, then turn N2 overspeed shutdown ON. Keep the independent N1 and engine-temperature protections from Build 2. If using N2 fuel limiting, its gradual-reduction band must sit below this trip with operating margin around the normal target. Start with the Simple method and review its reduction authority. Predictive uses acceleration as well and requires separate validation. Do not clear a retained limit merely to disable automatic shutdown; use the enable switch. Check: inject a safely simulated approach and overspeed. Confirm instrument colour/status, actual commanded fuel cut and the named fault. Repeat with N1 held steady to distinguish the two sources. The governor is ordinary regulation; its existence does not replace independent overspeed protection.

search.title: 3 · Convert the fuel controller into an N2 governor
search.context: Build 3 Add a free power turbine
search.text: The example uses a load capable of absorbing power from the free turbine. Below the target, more fuel tends to add turbine power; above it, less fuel reduces power. A disconnected or suddenly removed load can accelerate the free turbine rapidly. Do not test a real load rejection until its physical setup and independent protection are ready. Open the existing Main Fuel controller. Edit this controller rather than creating a second owner of Main Fuel Metering. Change its method from mapping to Hold a feedback target: | Field | Teaching setup | | --- | --- | | Controller name | Main Fuel N2 Governor | | Controlled output | Main Fuel Metering | | Feedback signal | N2 Power Shaft | | How is the target selected? | Fixed value | | Target | RPM | | Minimum / maximum output | % / % teaching fuel authority | | Activate when | Entering Running | | Deactivate when | Entering Shutdown and Entering Standby | Open Response tuning. Set Target deadband, Immediate response, Correction rate and Feedback-loss output from controlled testing of the actual plant. The response fields use percentages per measured unit, so RPM-scale gains are very different from pressure-scale gains. Record both the displayed units and the resulting command change. Do not tune using an unrelated oil controller's numbers. Re-enter the output bounds after changing method or source: the UI can initialize method-specific defaults. Check every field in the table before saving rather than assuming the previous mapping's range was retained. The earlier automatic idle is a Running fuel floor, not a second governor. For the first N2-governor exercise, set Fuel-metering support → Idle → Off and verify the governor's permitted minimum sustains the core in the actual operating envelope. The example starts with its % stable-idle command as the lower bound, rather than treating the % reliable pump minimum as an engine-idle guarantee. Reintroduce an idle floor only after checking how it constrains N2 control, especially during load rejection. Startup fuel and starter-release checks remain explicit in Sequence. With Fixed value, the throttle knob no longer directly sets fuel. That is intentional for this fixed-speed teaching load. For variable speed demand, later choose Variable input, Target input = Throttle Input, its 0–100% endpoints and separately verified low/high N2 target speeds. Those target values are RPM, not fuel percentages. A fixed-speed generator and a variable-speed load should not silently share one demand interpretation. Check: below/above-target test feedback moves fuel in the intended direction while respecting output bounds. Check target acquisition, deadband, sustained error and sensor loss. Simulated input changes demonstrate command logic; stability and load response need the real constrained mechanical system.

search.title: 4 · Review startup and ownership again
search.context: Build 3 Add a free power turbine
search.text: Startup first establishes lubrication, gas-generator speed and combustion. Starting the free turbine under load may require different N1/fuel conditions from the original turbojet. Do not assume the unchanged Build 1 fuel schedule will reach a loaded power-turbine target. 1. In Sequence → Startup, review the existing fuel commands and N1 checks against the new load. Keep all evidence waits finite. 2. Open Final Startup Checks. If startup must establish a minimum N2 before Running, select Require N2, enter that verified minimum and review the overall timeout. Do not use the maximum governed speed as a minimum-start check. 3. With the governor activated on Entering Running, Sequence controls startup fuel until that handover. Check its entry command and authority for an unwanted fuel step. 4. Review Shutdown: governor deactivation releases fuel to its safe demand, the cut block isolates combustion, and the required oil systems continue while shafts slow. Gas-generator N1 reaching zero does not prove the free turbine is stopped. If a controller must take over before Running, use the sequencer activation procedure from Build 2. While it owns an output, conflicting discrete sequence commands are ghosted. Place deactivation before a later discrete command that needs that output. | Phase | Fuel authority | Checks to retain | | --- | --- | --- | | Startup | Explicit sequence commands until chosen activation event | Oil, light-off, acceleration, finite timeout | | Running | Main Fuel N2 Governor, bounded by protections | N1, N2, temperature, oil and sensor health | | Shutdown | Deactivation safe state, combustion cut and shutdown handling | Physical fuel isolation and both shafts' lubrication needs | | Fault | Authoritative fault/protective handling | Actual output states, recorded reason and recovery condition |

search.title: 5 · Verify the second-shaft behavior
search.context: Build 3 Add a free power turbine
search.text: Keep hazardous energy isolated for command tests; use test signals or the simulator. Record real mechanical commissioning separately. - Check N1/N2 identities, PPR and any gearbox conversion independently. - Check normal handover, governor direction, output bounds and loss of N2. - Simulate an increase in N2 representing loss of load; verify fuel reduction and independent overspeed response. This does not physically qualify load rejection. - Confirm temperature/N1 constraints can reduce the governor's requested fuel. - Repeat STOP, failed-start timeout, shutdown and configured oil-loss policies. - Review lubrication for a free turbine that may continue spinning after the core stops. Add an independently configured oil circuit or windmilling protection if required by the design, and test its own shaft source. - Save/reload and download Build 3 — free power turbine, with a short list of completed and pending physical tests. At this point, you should be able to identify every measurement, controller and protection without following a different recipe for each one. That is the transferable skill: check the interface → add Hardware → calibrate → define control → test normal and failed behavior → back up.

search.title: 6 · Choose useful instruments
search.context: Build 3 Add a free power turbine
search.text: Add only what helps your installation. These are independent optional workshops, not requirements for finishing this build: | Addition | What you learn | | --- | --- | | Oil temperature and cooling fan | Temperature input, hysteresis, activation and fault-safe behavior | | Battery voltage / current | Conditioned analogue measurements, zero and sensitivity | | Cover-status switch | Digital polarity and the difference between status and an actual interlock | | Shaft torque | Two pickups on the same torque-carrying shaft, running zero and calibrated twist | | Thrust | I²C discovery, load-cell zero, known reference and force units | Two speeds on different shafts do not measure torque. For power calculation, torque and speed must refer to the same shaft. Instruments also need their own mechanical mounting and calibration; a plausible display alone does not prove them. Looking for an earlier instrument section? Its full instructions are now in Optional instruments and bench workshops. ← Build 2 Optional workshops Detailed reference

search.title: Learn OpenTurbine with three guided builds
search.text: Configure one HX80-sized teaching engine as a basic turbojet, improve its control, then add a free power turbine using three manageable guided builds.

search.title: One example that grows
search.context: Learn OpenTurbine with three guided builds
search.text: The teaching engine is a homemade HX80-sized liquid-fuel turbine with ECU-controlled starter, spark ignition, fuel and oil delivery. Build 1 operates conceptually as a turbojet. Build 3 adds a mechanically separate free power turbine and load. Normal full-power N1 is about 60000 RPM, combustor pressure 3–4 bar and oil supply 4–5 bar. These describe the example, not every engine. The worksheet identifies which other numbers are teaching assumptions and which must come from your actual hardware. Each task follows connect → configure → calibrate where needed → check. A later build reuses the earlier inventory. You do not need every supported sensor or every control method to finish the guide.

search.title: Prepare once
search.context: Learn OpenTurbine with three guided builds
search.text: Use Get Started to install OpenTurbine, then choose the appropriate development-board pin column and parts. The main instructions use device and terminal names so the method transfers between boards. PCB profiles have their own labelled connections. Begin with hazardous load energy disconnected and suitable test loads/signals. Verify physical interfaces and command behavior before a live engine attempt. The independent physical stop and the engine's required lubrication/protection apply from Build 1. Keep notes identifying physical tests versus simulated checks. Keep one live ECU browser session at a time; reading this guide in another tab is fine. Select a screenshot or diagram to enlarge it. Every required setting is described in text too. Hide walkthrough screenshots gives a shorter reading view while keeping wiring diagrams visible.

search.title: Choose a milestone, not every feature
search.context: Learn OpenTurbine with three guided builds
search.text: - New to electronics or OpenTurbine: start at Build 1 and verify each task before continuing. - Already have the basic installation: compare its checklist and save a backup before entering Build 2. - Adding a free turbine: finish the control/protection baseline before Build 3. - Adding a specific instrument: use the optional workshops for current, battery, fan, switch, torque or thrust. They are not a fourth required build. Use the User Guide for alternative methods and field-by-field detail, the Hardware reference for interfaces, and Troubleshooting when a check fails. Begin with the basic turbojet →

search.title: Optional instruments and bench workshops
search.text: Add battery and current monitoring, a temperature-controlled fan, switch status, shaft torque or thrust when your OpenTurbine installation needs them.

search.title: Choose an addition
search.text: Complete the relevant guided build first. Each workshop below is independent: you do not need every sensor to finish Build 3. Reuse existing channels instead of adding duplicates, and reserve pins against your actual board inventory. The numbered GPIO examples in these workshops belong to the optional no-PSRAM ESP32-S3 extension plan in Parts and connections. They are not Classic pin assignments. The separate brightness/light project is a low-power bench exercise, not an engine-control requirement. Back to the three builds · Field-by-field User Guide

search.title: Measure a 12 V battery
search.text: Recognize the pattern: a divider reduces battery voltage to an ADC-safe measurement. This example measures a 12 V nominal battery, disconnected from its charger, starter and all inductive loads, with the measured source bounded to 0–16 V. Start with a current-limited adjustable supply to check the circuit, then use the isolated battery with a fused sensing lead. Nominal 12 V does not mean the battery always measures exactly 12 V. Use 68 kΩ above the ADC node, 12 kΩ from the node to GND, both 1%, and 100 nF from the node to GND. Source negative and ECU reference ground join deliberately. The fuse belongs close to battery positive; a battery can deliver dangerous fault current even when the sensing circuit draws very little. | Source voltage | Nominal ADC-node voltage | | --- | --- | | 12.0 V | 1.80 V | | 14.4 V | 2.16 V | | 16.0 V maximum for this exercise | 2.40 V | The hardware ratio is 12 / (68 + 12) = 0.15. The UI asks for the reciprocal: Voltage divider ratio = (68 + 12) / 12 = 6.6667. The card may display 6.67. Battery volts = measured ADC-pin volts × this ratio. The ADC's measurable range depends on target and attenuation; it is not simply the GPIO's maximum electrical voltage. Check the Espressif ADC documentation for the selected target and verify the node with a meter before connecting GPIO. Configure: add Battery voltage, name it Battery Voltage, choose Analog voltage input (ADC), and use GPIO 4 in the cumulative S3 plan. Enter 6.6667 for Voltage divider ratio, leave analog input bias off, and keep the measured-signal validity window consistent with this 0–2.4 V circuit. Save and reopen. Verify: compare the source with a trusted meter at two or more known voltages and compare the node with the table. Correct scale using the actual resistor ratio and measured calibration; do not hide a wiring or saturation problem with a multiplier. Disconnect the sensing lead with the circuit safe and inspect the reading/health. A disconnected divider may read zero rather than identify an open wire; this is not a supervised battery sensor. An enabled ADC input with no sensor or divider attached floats: its value and trend can jump even though the channel appears healthy. Disable unfitted devices in Hardware. If readings fluctuate with the circuit connected, check ground, wiring, supply noise and calibration; do not assume it is normal or conceal it with averaging. For a live engine bus: do not carry this bare divider into starter, alternator, ignition or switched-pump wiring. Load dump, inductive spikes, reverse polarity, ground offset and pin back-power require a properly rated protected measurement front end. Size that interface for maximum voltage and credible faults, not the battery label. Reuse the software steps and verified scale only after checking that interface. Decide whether this is monitoring only or an enabled low-supply protection. On Controllers → Shutdown & Protection → Auxiliary Protection → Low supply voltage, choose the actual threshold, confirmation time and enable state only after measurement is proven. There is no universal low-voltage trip suitable for every battery chemistry and oil/cooling arrangement.

search.title: Measure current
search.text: Recognize the pattern: an analog voltage can represent amps. This exercise uses an INA180A1 shunt amplifier on a small fused 5 V load, limited to 0–1 A. Use a 0.1 Ω shunt rated at least 0.5 W, gain 20, 3.3 V amplifier supply and 100 nF local bypass. Nominal output sensitivity is 20 × 0.1 = 2 V/A, so 1 A gives about 2 V. Actual offset and sensitivity need calibration. For the cumulative example, open Oil Pump on Hardware and its Current sensing subcard. Enable sensing and choose the separate current ADC pin. Enter the sensor's zero voltage and sensitivity at the ECU pin: the nominal sensitivity of this exact bounded circuit is 2000 mV/A, not the value shown for a different Hall sensor. Save and use the available Calibration wizard to capture zero and a known reference where offered. When learning, measure a separate benign load through the shunt while the real pump power is disconnected; label this as a demonstration reading. It does not measure or validate the real oil pump until installed in that actual path. You can instead add a General current analog channel for a separate instrument, but do not assign the same physical ADC pin twice. Verify: compare with a trusted current meter at zero and a known load. Near-zero offsets and noise are normal measurement considerations. A negative/reversed sense connection or the wrong amplifier gain invalidates the calculation. Decide whether overcurrent protection is enabled; a zero shutdown threshold disables that output's overcurrent trip in the current UI. Do not choose a trip from the dummy load's rating and carry it into a real pump. The shunt circuit is not isolated and does not size high-power pump/starter conductors or transient protection. A different module can have a 5 V analog output even when its listing says “current sensor”; condition it before GPIO.

search.title: Add temperature and a cooling fan
search.text: Add temperature: use a three-wire DS18B20 for an oil/enclosure temperature lesson. It uses a separate OneWire data GPIO and external 4.7 kΩ pull-up. It is not a turbine-gas temperature sensor. Confirm the probe pinout and physical temperature rating. Add Oil Temp, purpose Oil / gearbox temperature, with the DS18B20 interface and actual GPIO. Save. Check a plausible room reading, gentle warming and input health before using it as control feedback. Add the fan: use a suitably rated PWM fan driver or on/off interface, reusing the PWM or relay pattern. Add Cooling Fan, purpose Cooling fan, with the real driver, pin and safe demand. Keep the output unowned before creating its custom controller. A four-wire fan with a dedicated PWM input has different wiring from a two-wire fan whose supply is switched—follow its documentation. On Controllers → Output controllers, expand + Create controller, choose Cooling Fan, create it and open its card. Choose method On / Off with hysteresis, source Oil Temp, and the required above-threshold relationship. The output command values must suit the chosen driver. Choose the events that activate and deactivate it. For a benign warming exercise, you might demonstrate on above 30 °C, off again below 28 °C, using 2 °C hysteresis. These are observation values for the bench probe, not oil/cooling limits for an engine. Hysteresis prevents chatter around one threshold. Find the threshold fields: choose On / Off with hysteresis to expose Controlled by, Direction, Switch point and Hysteresis. Select Oil Temp, then Turn on above. Review the on/off commands for the fitted fan driver. For this bench lesson choose Activate when → Entering Standby and Deactivate when → Entering Startup, Entering Running, Entering Shutdown directly in the open card. Test the next appropriate state entry and save using the same change recap as Build 2. Verify: raise and lower the measured temperature around both boundaries, then check STANDBY, STARTUP, RUNNING and SHUTDOWN as applicable. Check deactivation, unplugged sensor and FAULT behavior too. Deactivation sends Hardware safe demand before release; custom controllers are also released in FAULT, whose protective output handling remains authoritative. Do not assume cooling continues through a fault. If cooling is essential, design the complete physical and software loss response for that requirement.

search.title: Add a cover switch
search.text: Recognize the pattern: a dry contact becomes a digital state. Connect a maintenance-cover switch between its GPIO and GND. On a pin with internal bias, choose Pull-up and active-low in Hardware; this short bench circuit needs no external resistor. Alternatively, wire the contact to 3.3 V and choose Pull-down and active-high. Use an external bias resistor where the pin lacks internal bias or the wiring needs stronger conditioning. Add Cover closed, purpose Digital interlock, driver On/off switch input. Use the actual pin and active polarity. For closed-is-active in the shown wiring, select active-low. Verify the displayed input state while opening and closing the switch. Choose whether “active” means cover closed or cover open and name it accordingly; do not rely on the word interlock alone to create an action. For the lesson, use it as a visible status/custom-controller source. If the actual purpose is to block startup, review the separate Inhibit-start switch role and the current documented DI behavior rather than assuming any generic switch automatically prevents START. Use only one saved assignment for each physical input. Verify both states and disconnect a wire. A simple single-contact circuit may confuse an open wire with one ordinary state; it is not a supervised safety circuit. An ECU-connected emergency-stop input is also not the independent physical stop. Keep that distinction when adapting the switch pattern to other functions.

search.title: Measure shaft torque with two pickups
search.text: What this measures: the angular twist between two points on the same torque-carrying shaft. OpenTurbine measures the phase difference between matching conditioned pulse trains, removes the calibrated running zero and converts shaft degrees to Nm. These are two pickups on one shaft, not the N1 and N2 speeds of different shafts. Two RPM values alone cannot supply torque. Wire it: use two conditioned 3.3 V square-wave pickups at mechanically defined points along the shaft. Connect their reference grounds as their conditioners require; reference output goes to one spare input GPIO and phase output to another. The cumulative S3 example reserves GPIO 41 and 42. Both wheels must produce the same effective pulses per shaft revolution, including gearing. Unmatched, unindexed tooth counts are rejected; a static tooth offset cannot correct them. This interface uses native capture inputs and needs no SPI or I²C bus. Configure Hardware: 1. Choose Add input → Torque, open the Torque card, then select Sensor interface → Shaft torsion by phase difference (two pickups). 2. In Reference shaft pickup, choose Reference GPIO and set Reference pulses per shaft revolution to the actual target count. 3. In Torque phase pickup, choose Phase GPIO and set Torque pickup pulses per shaft revolution to the matching effective count. 4. In this cumulative example leave Use reference as shaft speed (optional) unchecked: N1 and N2 already have their own fitted speed sensors. If you need another speed role in a different installation, confirm it saves without a conflict rather than duplicating a primary shaft assignment. 5. Use a trusted previously measured Zero-torque phase (shaft degrees) and Sensitivity (shaft degrees / Nm), or complete the calibration below. A placeholder sensitivity is not a calibrated torque reading. Save and reopen the card. Calibrate: use a suitable rotating test rig with independent torque reference. Open Calibration → Torque, spin at verified zero load and select Capture zero phase. Keep the shaft rotating, apply known torque, enter Known torque (Nm) and select Capture known torque. Static alignment is not a running zero. Captures made while RUNNING are staged in that browser tab: stop and choose Save captured calibration in STANDBY to apply them. The ECU does not change calibration mid-run. A working result: zero-load torque stays near zero at several speeds; known loads produce the expected sign and Nm across the usable range. If calculating shaft power, the selected speed must belong to the same measured torque-carrying shaft; verify it independently. Loss of the phase pickup must invalidate torque; a healthy reference may still provide configured speed telemetry. Loss of the reference invalidates the phase calculation. Keep torque trips and fuel limiting off until the measurement is proven.

search.title: Measure thrust with an I²C load cell
search.text: What we are adding: a mechanically mounted thrust load cell and NAU7802 bridge amplifier. The amplifier reads the small bridge signal and sends data over I²C. Thrust uses force in newtons, while torque uses Nm. Select a load cell with the required range and mounting arrangement; the wiring does not define the mechanical test stand. Wire it: with power removed, connect the bridge excitation to E+ / E− and its differential signal to A+ / A− on the module. Connect the documented 3.3 V-compatible module supply and reference ground to the ECU. Connect SDA and SCL to separate spare bus GPIOs (GPIO 11 / 47 in the cumulative S3 plan). Use SDA/SCL pull-ups to 3.3 V appropriate for the bus; many breakouts already include them. Check the module circuit before adding more resistors. The dry-contact internal-bias lesson does not replace I²C bus pull-ups. Activate the bus before adding the sensor: 1. Open Hardware → Shared sensor buses → Edit buses and turn on Enable shared I2C bus. 2. Select SDA GPIO and SCL GPIO to match the wires; start with 100 kHz bus speed. Save and let the ECU restart. 3. Return to the bus section and confirm NAU7802 appears as a detected, connected device. The typical address is 0x2A. If it is missing, check power, SDA/SCL, pull-ups and address before adding an assignment. 4. Choose Add input → Thrust, open the card and choose NAU7802 load cell. Select the detected device and the bridge channel actually wired. Save. Only a detected chip can receive a new assignment. Calibrate: open Calibration → Thrust. With the complete stand unloaded, select Capture zero. Apply a known force or mass in the measurement direction, enter Known load, and choose the matching Unit: for example N for force or kg mass for mass. Select Capture known load & save. Remove the reference load and check the return to zero, then test a second known load. If the sign is wrong, correct the signal polarity or signed calibration as offered by the interface and repeat the check. A working result: the dashboard reports near-zero N unloaded, the known test forces agree with the reference, and the reading returns to zero after unloading. Disconnect the amplifier with loads made safe and confirm the input becomes unhealthy rather than retaining a believable live force. This addition is measurement only until you deliberately configure another relationship. Using both measurements: the phase pickups and I²C load cell use different interfaces and can coexist with the earlier N1/N2 sensors. The example reserves their pins separately. A fixed-address NAU7802 cannot share one unmodified bus with a second device at the same address; check address compatibility before adding another bridge amplifier.

search.title: Optional bench exercise: build a light-dimming controller
search.text: Useful result: a separate brightness knob adjusts a low-power bench light. Turning the knob from minimum through midpoint to maximum changes the PWM demand from 0% through 50% to 100%. It uses a general-purpose input and output; it does not commandeer fuel, starter or oil hardware. Wire the knob: reuse the potentiometer pattern with a second 10 kΩ potentiometer. Its outer terminals go to 3.3 V and GND; the wiper goes to a spare ADC1 input, GPIO 8 in this cumulative S3 plan. Choose Hardware → Add input → Generic analog input, name it Brightness knob, and choose Analog voltage input (ADC). Leave internal pull-up/down off. Calibrate the actual endpoints; the example normalized source range is 0–1. Use Invert input if clockwise movement reduces the intended brightness. For this generic input, inspect its measured endpoints and the Minimum valid signal / Maximum valid signal fields on the Hardware card. Set the electrical range to the verified endpoint readings so the normalized value spans 0–1; test the middle as well. Do not assume the dedicated Throttle calibration wizard edits this separate generic input. Wire the light: reuse the PWM-driver pattern with a documented 3.3 V-compatible MOSFET driver and separately supplied low-power dimmable LED module or suitable small lamp. Use the lamp/module's specified current limiting—do not connect a bare LED directly to a power supply or GPIO. This is low-voltage DC only, not a mains dimmer. Choose Hardware → Add output → PWM output, name it Bench light, choose PWM and the spare output GPIO 38. The fixture uses 1000 Hz, 10 bits, normal direction and 0–100% electrical duty endpoints. Set Power-on demand to 0%. Verify physical off at logical zero before permitting the controller to own it. A · Create the controller. Open Controllers → Output controllers → + Create controller. Choose Bench light in What do you want to control?, then select Create controller. An absent output may be unfitted, incompatible or already owned; resolve that instead of duplicating it. B · Open its card. A new generic controller starts with Fixed output and zero command. Change the method to Map input to output before looking for the source and range fields. C · Configure the complete mapping: | Field | This bench example | | --- | --- | | Controller name | Brightness control | | Controlled output | Bench light | | Control method | Map input to output | | Controlled by | Brightness knob | | Input low / Input high | 0 / 1, after verified endpoint calibration | | Output low / Output high | 0% / 100% | | Active when | Entering Standby | | Deactivate when | Entering Startup, Entering Running, Entering Shutdown | D · Choose activation and deactivation. The open controller card directly shows both sets of choices. Select Entering Standby under Active when; select Entering Startup, Entering Running and Entering Shutdown under Deactivate when. Clear the default Running activation. State entries are events, not continuous mode checkboxes: the light follows the knob after its selected entry until a selected stop event. Test the next appropriate state entry; saving while already in Standby does not invent that entry. E · Save and reopen. Select Save to device, resolve any validation errors and review warnings rather than using Save anyway to get past them. Confirm the change recap, save, then reopen the card and compare output, source, range and states. Verify: low knob gives a physically off light, midpoint gives about 50% duty, and high gives full permitted duty. Check clamping beyond calibrated endpoints, smooth movement, direction, mode exit, input loss and reboot behavior. Confirm the light's power-on state and that no controller accidentally claims an engine output. A failed potentiometer may leave a plausible ADC voltage; an unsupervised knob is not a safety input. Adapt the lesson: an external noncritical fan can use the same mapping, but use its own driver and permitted PWM frequency. A fan may need a nonzero minimum reliable command and separate start behavior; do not assume the light's 0–100% duty range will start or safely stop every fan. Feedback regulation is a different method: Hold a feedback target needs a verified measured result and failure response.

search.context: Guided-build parts, connections and engine worksheet
search.text: Use this as a record, not an installation preset. Operating anchors come from the example brief. Assumed values make the lesson concrete; they have not been measured on an HX80 engine. Measured interface values come from your sensor, driver, calibration rig and engine. A turbocharger model does not determine a fuel schedule. | Quantity | Teaching example | Source / what to record for your engine | | --- | --- | --- | | Normal full-power N1 | RPM | Operating anchor; record actual shaft and independently measured speed | | Normal combustor pressure | 3–4 bar gauge | Operating anchor; identify tap and reference | | Normal oil supply | 4–5 bar gauge | Operating anchor; identify where measured and oil temperature | | Nominal oil target | bar | Midpoint example; validate supply, flow and bearing requirements | | N1 idle / maximum trip | / RPM | Assumed teaching values; establish actual stable idle and permissible limit independently | | Normal TOT / running trip | / °C | Assumed; identify exact probe location and actual engine limits | | Separate startup trip / sustained threshold | °C / °C for ms | Assumed transient envelope; justify before using | | Pre-start maximum / light-off confirmation | / °C | Assumed; different jobs, not interchangeable | | Reliable fuel minimum / idle / full command | / / % | Assumed pump results, not transferable flow or power percentages | | Pre-ignition N1 / starter demand | RPM / % | Assumed; verify actual airflow, starter and coupling | | Oil minimum / confirmation | bar / ms | Assumed; check bearing requirements and all enabled oil-failure sources | | P1 limiting begin / full / shutdown | / / bar | Assumed; preserve operating margin, not sensor full scale | | N2 target / hard trip | / RPM | Assumed for a separate teaching power shaft; include gearing if sensed elsewhere | Record fuel type, nozzle/flow calibration, pump/ESC models, temperature-probe position, actual starter release, all finite wait timeouts, oil cooldown requirements and each failed-sensor response alongside this table. It is not a validated homemade turbojet start schedule. Treat the guide's assumed numbers accordingly.

search.title: A worked pressure conversion
search.context: Guided-build parts, connections and engine worksheet
search.text: For a documented 0.5–4.5 V, 0–10 bar gauge transducer, the 15 kΩ upper / 10 kΩ lower divider multiplies output by 0.4: | Pressure | Sensor output | ADC-pin voltage | | --- | --- | --- | | 0 bar | 0.50 V | 0.20 V | | 3.5 bar | 1.90 V | 0.76 V | | 4.5 bar | 2.30 V | 0.92 V | | 10 bar | 4.50 V | 1.80 V | ADC zero is mV and sensitivity mV/bar. The sensor's 10 bar span, the oil controller's 4.5 bar target and a low-pressure fault limit are three different settings. Measure and calibrate the actual circuit. A resistor divider alone does not provide installation-level fault or transient protection.
